utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning, Witness. Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before your cross-examination, could I ask you how long are you going to take for your cross-examination for this witness. The reason I'm asking you about the time is that the Bench has to decide whether we have an extra sitting on Thursday afternoon if we could not finish all the witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's two matters to -- in reply. Firstly, as to the cross-examination of Mr. Dzankovic, I should think an hour and a half will complete what I have to ask. It may go slightly longer, but I expect not, frankly. I think it will be an hour and a half. But, however, there is another issue about that. We understand that the -- the next two witnesses listed here, one -- one is a very short witness. The next one is Mr. Hodzic. We just haven't been provided with the notes and the -- you know, the materials that we need in relation to him, so I can't say whether we're ready or not in respect of that witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honour. Your Honour, we are ready with the next witness that's -- the short witness that's directly after this witness here. We would not be ready for Mr. Hodzic until tomorrow morning -- until tomorrow morning. He came in later than we expected. We met him for the first time yesterday, and we would need today. We would take one day in examination-in-chief, which would be Wednesday. If this Court would like to run an extra session into Thursday afternoon, if cross-examination could be one, even one and a half days, if you had a three-hour afternoon session Thursday afternoon, we could complete Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections for the extra session on Thursday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's -- I don't have any objections to an extra session at all. And that's regardless of whether we would finish. It is for the witness's benefit to finish, if we can. But I should tell you that as responsible counsel, I just couldn't tell you yet whether I'm going to be finished in that time. It -- he's a witness in respect of whom I'm -- I expect, although I haven't been told yet, that -- that there may be an attempt to lead certain books into evidence through him. Now, if those books are the subject of cross-examination, he'll definitely go two days and he might go three. If -- if they're not, then it's going to be considerably shorter, frankly. But at the moment, we don't have the list, so I don't -- I don't know, Your Honour. What I'd like is that as soon as I get the relevant materials from the Prosecutor, to have a moment to consider those and then advise the Court straight away, because if we can finish it, then we're very happy to cooperate and we will accommodate the Court. If you wish to sit an extra session, we'll be ready for that and we'll do it. But at the moment, I just don't know what I'm dealing with, frankly, as of yet. I'm ready to meet the witness in other respects. So it's to be hoped that we could complete him in that time. The Prosecution aren't -- it's not a doomed question. But I'd just like to know where I stand first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. It is in the interests of justice that the Bench should avoid a witness under the oath left for about a week's time, you know, because during that period the witness might go back to his home place. So there might be a danger of contamination of that witness, especially during the middle of his testimony. So we'll try our best to avoid this situation. But anyway, you may proceed with this witness in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. Dzankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown MFI221.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzankovic, they're going to bring up on the screen now a copy of the -- the report that you made, that being the second report to Jusuf Jasarevic, dated the 13th of September. And I'm just going to ask you to -- to recall what you can recall about some specific topics from that report. So I'll just wait till it's -- till you have it.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Very well. Now, I just have some questions for you as to the sources of information on which you compiled this document. I take it you compiled this document partly based on what you yourself saw and also partly based on what you were told by other people, by way of operative information, whether it's from the civilian police side or from -- from the military side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly I gathered the information with the help of the gentlemen from the public security station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I just wanted to ask you some questions. You received some help in your time in Jablanica from Mr. Brankovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. In a -- in about ten minutes, I'm going to turn to Mr. Brankovic and ask you the sort of help that you gave and what you did together. But at the moment I just -- I just have some questions about -- about the information here. Now, you've indicated that the -- the very first line: "On the 8th of September," that "units from Sarajevo arrived with Commander Ramiz Delalic." Now, was that information that -- well, I take it that was information that you knew yourself. That's not information from the civilian police. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw Mr. Delalic personally on one occasion in Zulfikar Alispago's base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the next paragraph -- you begin the paragraph by saying: "The units were quartered in Croatian houses on the right bank of the river." And I take it that you put that in the report because that's what you saw yourself with your own two eyes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say that they will, but I wrote down that they already had. As far as I know, they were already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. No, pardon me. I -- that was my error, not yours. I agree. Now, when you went on in the third -- the next section to talk about the treatment of the local population by the Zulfikar unit and Jablanica military civilian authorities, I take it you relied on information from the police and local authorities in order to put that in your report. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And by the way, you feel free, if -- if a question seems to be ambiguous or misleading, you point that out to me here because otherwise I won't know that I'm asking a bad question. All right. Well, now, there's another section -- I'm not sure whether it's on the first page of your text, but I think it is, and it reads: "In the morning of the 9th of September, the news spread that members" -- it's a bit hard to read, but that "members from Sarajevo had slaughtered the Croatian population. After having been informed of this by two Muslim refugees from Capljina, the chief of the Jablanica SJB, Emin Zebic, contacted Edib Saric, who confirmed that several" - and it's a bit hard to read again - "happened on the right bank of the Neretva, but he did not know the scale of it or the persons who perpetrated it." Now, once again, that information was information that you got from the police themselves; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zebic is not from the military security. He's from the public security service in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And then in the next section, you describe a visit by the Jablanica SJB deputy and the military police commander from Jablanica, and you've indicated what it was that they saw when they got to Grabovica. Now, once again, was that information that you got from the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Do you recall Mr. -- a man called Mr. Sead Kurt, who was the military police commander in question?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have the opportunity to meet him, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Now, continuing through that document, it's indicated then that -- and this is -- I'm just not sure where it is on the Bosnian document, but there's a reference there -- perhaps you could find it for me. It's probably about 20 lines down below where I was just looking, where there's a reference to Zuka writing a report on the incident. Do you -- just -- if you would just find that section for me, where it says: "Please note that only Zuka could enter these areas without consequences. He wrote a report on the incident and he will forward it to the Sarajevo SVK." Do you have that passage?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain --

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one second, please. Could you please scroll the text down, because it's not on the screen, that part. I have the beginning on my screen, so could you please scroll the text down so that I can try and find that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think that's now being done. Would you indicate when you've got the part that you want.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll it up a little bit now because it's too far. I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Can I just ask you about where you got that information. Is that something that the police told you, or is that something that Zuka himself told you?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Zuka told me that, actually. He said it at the meeting when we were all together at his place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: What did he tell you about that report that he wrote?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he just made the report. He wasn't really specific about what he said, and he didn't tell us anything about what he put in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Did Zuka indicate -- you've put in the report here that he -- "He will forward it to the Sarajevo SVK." Did he indicate who at the Sarajevo SVK -- and sorry, perhaps I should take a step back. "SVK" means the General Staff, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Whereas, the security administration, which you were involved in, is the SVB; correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the reason I make these qualifications is that we have a lot of these acronyms to deal with in this case, so we just need to clarify. Anyway, what -- what Zulfikar Alispago was telling you is that he was going to send this report to the General Staff in Sarajevo. And what I wanted to ask you: Did he -- did he get specific about who at the General Staff he was going to send it to in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're thinking whether he mentioned any person specifically or not, no, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Did he mention what was in the report? Did he tell you what the contents of the report was?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that. He wasn't specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. There are just some details I have to ask you about because of other evidence that's been given in the case, so bear with me. Did he mention whether or not he was including in the report any photographs or films taken by soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing of that for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. In fact, to your knowledge, was it ever suggested to you during the time when you were investigating this matter -- was it ever suggested to you that any soldiers had taken photographs or videos or films of any sort from the left bank of the Neretva at or around the time of these events? Was that ever suggested or mentioned to you in any way?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing this for the first time from you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. When you were speaking to Zuka about these matters at his flat, was this -- I take it this was before Ramiz Delalic and his large deputy, Malco, or his large -- his large companion, Malco, arrived. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. Because at the time when -- when Ramiz and Malco were present, it's fair to say that the discussion occurred very much between Zuka and Ramiz; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And, in fact, that discussion chiefly focussed upon Ramiz being angry about the investigation and Ramiz proposing to go back to Sarajevo with his troops; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ramiz was angry, and the gist of the conversation was that he wanted to return his units back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And in the course of that display of anger, he manifested a -- an attitude of resentment and anger against Bakir Alispahic and his unit, the Laste unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was angry because they left Jablanica and went to Mostar without telling anyone about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Well, look, I asked you this question yesterday, and I -- look, I won't repeat it. I'm sorry. I won't have another go at it. Okay. Very well. Now, as to that report by Zulfikar Alispago, however, nobody ever provided a copy of that report to you personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And shortly after this meeting in the flat, to your knowledge, Zulfikar Alispago departed in the direction of Vrdi to take part in the combat activities himself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, after the meeting, the next day or the day after -- actually, it was about a couple of days after that that all the units and the commanders left the area and went to where the combat operations were being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. And just in terms of the specific areas to -- to which people departed, to your knowledge there were combat operations both to the south and to the north of Jablanica; is that correct? One -- one lot of combat operations in the direction of Vrdi, in the south; and the other lot of -- of operations in the general direction of Prozor, in the north? Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where the combat activities were, but I heard that the combat activities would be conducted over a wide area, from Prozor to Mostar, in order to stretch out the enemy and weaken their strength in some places and to extend it over a broad area so that there would be some places vulnerable where it would be possible to break the lines. However, I'm not -- I don't know which specific territory or places these were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. And my questions to you are not really designed to ask you for commentary on the -- on the combat activities. All I wanted to limit it to you at this stage was this: As far as you knew, Zuka went south in the direction of Vrdi with his units.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, he went in that direction together with the units from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the time when Ramiz was present in that flat, did you say a single word to Ramiz yourself?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I take it your situation was one of relative -- well, I withdraw that. Did you observe Mr. Salihamidzic, who was sitting with you, also to keep very silent during the time when Ramiz was present?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, both him and Sejo Brankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And throughout the time he was present at that meeting, the behaviour of Ramiz Delalic appeared to you to be somewhat aggressive and intimidating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was angry. I -- I can't say that he threatened anybody amongst us, but it was a fact that he was angry, and this was. Nobody wanted to enter into a conversation with him when he was in that state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So far as you could observe, Zulfikar Alispago was effectively begging him not to take his troops back to Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And Zulfikar was saying to him -- I don't mean in these exact words, but words to the effect, "Look, Ramiz, there's a big crisis in Mostar. There are citizens in trouble. Our army is in trouble down there. The HVO are going to attack. We need you." Is that approximately what was said by -- by Zuka?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, along those lines. He said, "Don't go because of the people down there who are waiting for us to lift the blockade. They're starving." It was along these lines that he was making comments. And he said that it was necessary for him to help out in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And he told him that the operation would fail if -- Zuka told Ramiz in particular the operation would fail if he persisted with taking the troops back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And the discussion ended with -- with Ramiz saying that Bakir Alispahic and his Laste unit should go to Mostar, and then he turned with his friend Malco and walked out the door; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did mention that Bakir Alispahic with the Laste unit should go and lift the blockade of Mostar, but as far as I can recollect, we left the room before Ramiz, so I am not sure. I don't know what the end of the conversation was between Ramiz and Zuka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Okay. Well, during the time when you were present in that room, what you can say is that Zulfikar Alispago didn't issue any orders to Ramiz but, rather, pleaded with him and begged him to stay; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to keep going now with what you've said in the report, and I just ask you to -- to clarify certain matters in it. Could you move down now to the reference to a situation that -- that you learned about of a woman being raped -- or perhaps, sorry, no, before that, we'll get to the question of the murdered Croat. You say in the report: "I was informed that a certain Croat member of the Zulfikar special unit was killed." Now, I've just got a question about that: The -- in the English version that we've got, there's missing text there. Are you able to say what the word after -- the word before the word "Croat" is on the B/C/S copy that you've got?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't read it very well. I can see "I see" -- I don't know if it's a name, because it's in block letters "ICI" - sorry - "ICA." It's a photocopy, and the first couple of letters are missing, have been deleted, so I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, look, I'll put a name to you and you see -- apart from what's written here, you see if that jogs your memory. Does the name Ivica Kavlovic refresh your memory in any way?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, no, because I can't say that I know of him or anything, and the information about the person killed was given to me by Mr. Zuka and on that occasion he also told me the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. Okay. Well, what attitude did Zuka appear to take to the fact that one of his own soldiers had been murdered in relatively brutal circumstances?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I can conclude on the basis of the conversation we had on the spot, Zuka was basically angry and embittered and he did not approve of what had happened, what had happened to his soldier and to the other civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And to your knowledge, Zulfikar Alispago helped with evacuating civilians from the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I heard, and that he brought two boys to his base and he placed them under the protection of his soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And I want to -- I'll come to the two boys in just a moment, but in general terms, you -- the police told you that Zuka was cooperating, as far as their efforts were concerned, in dealing with this crisis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And, in fact, it was Zuka himself who invited you, Brankovic, and Salihamidzic to his flat that very night when this episode with Ramiz took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were sitting at CJB Jablanica and we were discussing what had happened, and then Mr. Zebic suggested, since the phones at Jablanica were working, he suggested that Salihamidzic should get in touch with Mr. Zuka, and he did that. And then he came back later and he said, "Zuka said to go to his flat. He's there, and we can talk."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Okay. Now, when you -- when you heard about the rescue of the two boys, did Zuka tell you that he'd provided security for these boys and, in particular, had provided a guard for these two boys to protect them once he brought them back to his base?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he took them out of Jablanica and he took them to his base, where they're safe. He didn't say anything specific as to whether he appointed any guards or anything. He said, "They're at my base and they're safe there."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, I want to move on to the next issue, and that is the issue of the raped woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is at the bottom of page 2, the top of page 3 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: If you need the -- the paper to be scrolled down, Mr. Dzankovic, would you just indicate that. But could you just look a couple of lines below the reference to Zuka. You'll see there's a reference to this: "Also a woman was raped and a rape of another woman was attempted on the left bank of the Neretva in the village where the refugees from Capljina are accommodated." Do you have that -- that passage?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, I just want to ask you something about the next part, you said -- you said this: "The service will interview the raped woman and take a statement -- take a written statement from her." Now, I just want to ask you about that. At the stage when you wrote the report, I take it that such a statement had yet to be taken. And what I wanted to ask you about was this: Was the raped woman prepared to give a statement when it came to it?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the statement -- or rather, first of all, the information about the raped woman and the attempted rape was the information that I got from the MUP members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And since it was about a civilian, the statement had to be taken by someone from SJB Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether this was done and whether the lady in question was willing to make a statement or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. The -- when you say that therefore, the reference in the English translation says here, "The service will interview the raped woman." By the words "the service," who did you mean? Did you mean the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand all right. Now, you then went on to say that -- that the Jablanica IKM, civilian authorities, and the MUP organs are aware of this incident. And I just wanted to ask you how you were able to say that the MUP organs were aware of the incident. Is that because the local police station knew about and it because Mr. Brankovic knew about it as well? Is that what the basis for that comment is?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you then went on to say that -- effectively that certain aspects of the investigation were currently impossible. I'll take you to that in detail. You say: "Work on the clarification of this case, gathering of operation -- operative information on the exact number of dead, how they were murdered, and detection of possible perpetrators has been done in cooperation with" and then there's an illegible part. Are you able to say what that word which is at the end of the phrase "detection of possible perpetrators has been done in cooperation with" -- what's the next word there? Can you translate that or tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't I can't see anything. Especially, it's a photocopy. It's totally black there. I can't read it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just excuse me one moment. I'll see if we've got a better original. Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzankovic, I might come back to that because I'll -- I'll try to get a hard copy. It may be that that's easier to read. Anyway, regardless of what's written there, the work of the clarification and of the case and so on was done in cooperation with the civilian authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to go on to the next bit. You say that "something on site" - and there's a word that's hard to translate there, and I'll ask you to tell us if you can work it out - "something on site is currently impossible to carry out because of the large number of units in the Grabovica area, the units led by Ramiz Delalic, and fear that giving too much" - sorry - "fear that giving importance to this incident would result in" - gap - "return of the whole unit to Sarajevo, which would directly endanger the planned action on Mostar." Now, I've read that at length. But I'll just ask you about a couple of aspects about it: Were you intending to convey by that report that a site inspection was currently impossible to carry out?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you then went on to list the reasons why that was impossible to carry out in a summary form; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, when you were referring to the attitude of units led by Ramiz Delalic, you were referring to a number of factors indicating aggressive and dangerous behaviour by those units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the entire units but the behaviour of those who were the perpetrators and who had we gone through, probably for their own protection and in order to cover up what had happened, would have probably attacked us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, that's -- thank you. But you've just answered my next series of questions. I mean, your fear was that, among other things, that if you went there to investigate, you may well be the subject of danger yourself from these apparently very dangerous individuals; is that true?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And it was a bit useless for me to go there on my own and try to do something. First of all, I wouldn't have been protected; and secondly, I'm not an expert. So on my own, I wouldn't have been able to achieve anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was there rumours at the time of a sniper being posted around the area of Grabovica?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that it was a rumour that there was a sniper there, but there was a rumour that if somebody were to set out down there, that there was a risk of a sniper, if anyone were to go down and try and carry out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I just want you to move a few lines down to the section where Ramiz Delalic was talking, and you've described the conversation that he had in Zuka's flat, at the bottom of this -- at that -- it's the last sentence in that section. And it says this: "He also said" -- and the "he" that you're talking about clearly is Ramiz Delalic. "He also said that there was real danger of possible open clashes between the" - missing text - "unit members and persons who would carry out the on-site inspection and possibly try to identify and arrest the perpetrators. So part of your problem was that Ramiz Delalic had said investigators who is go there might as well end up in a fight?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object. That's not listed there. Are you asking or are you indicating it says that there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to me that you put the answer in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I was putting is -- I put the proposition, which the witness is free to agree with or disagree with: So part of your problem was that Ramiz Delalic had said an investigator who is to go there might well end up in a fight." Now, I -- at the moment I'm simply mystified as to what the objection is. I can put that proposition to him. He can say "no" or "yes." What I've put to him -- and Your Honours, perhaps I -- I just want to make clear about this objection. It seems to be a new tactic here. But, Your Honours, I want to make it clear that I have to as a matter of fairness put to the witness the passages -- direct his attention to those before I ask the question; otherwise, I might be met with an objection that I'm not putting those to him in a fair and reasonable way. That's what I was doing. If the Prosecutor is concerned about the question, the question is the part that's at the very end, and that is the part to which any objection, if there remains an objection, ought to be taken. But that proposition, in my submission, seems, I hope, to be a rather cautiously put one and not an unfair one. Now, if the Prosecutor objects to that last part, then it should be articulated concerning that last part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, strictly the objection concerns the form of the question. I am not objecting to him asking about that area. The form of the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And for the record, we have objected far less than the Defence have objected in this case, Your Honour. And the record is clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's -- that's quite true. The Defence has had occasion to object many more times than the Prosecutor. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you could put your question another way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It sounds like that's the best -- the best answer, Your Honour. We will. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Mr. Dzankovic, I'm going to try again now, and I'll deal with it differently. One of the reasons why you were concerned about -- or one of the -- sorry, perhaps -- I take that back. One of the problems facing any attempt to conduct an on-site investigation was that Ramiz Delalic said that there could be a fight between soldiers in Grabovica and the investigators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, what you're asking is something that I can't see anywhere. I can't see a reference to the fact that Ramiz said something, but it is a fact that if an investigation team were to go down there, there would have been a conflict. That was my assessment at that time, and I'm -- I still stand by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, I just want to be fair to you, Mr. Dzankovic, and make sure that you have the opportunity to see what I base the question on. Do you see a sentence here which says: "Ramiz Delalic said as much. While discussing this incident in Zuka's apartment, the following persons were present at this discussion." And then there's a list. Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can see that. But you should read it again from the beginning, because if you look at it within context, you can see that it was him announcing that he and his units would leave Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. And it's just the -- the sentence following that. Do you see word "Sejo Brankovic" there?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. It's the sentence after I'm asking about. I accept your answer. I just don't want you to be under a misapprehension about why I asked.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, see, what it says in the text is whey did say, in fact. My comment is that I expected there to be a conflict. And with respect to what Ramiz Delalic had said, it was about the units going back. And well, the conclusions are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Now, I just want to move on to the next section now. This is where you say in your report: "The situation in Grabovica is currently under control, which is due to Delalic executing one of his own soldiers after these incidents." Now, what led you to think that Delalic had executed one of his own soldiers after these incidents? In other words, what was your source of information that this had happened?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what he himself said when he came to Zuka's place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did he say anything about performing a line-up or an identity parade of any sort when he was speaking to Zuka in the flat, or not?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About an actual line-up, no. He just came in and said, "Why do I need to have to shoot my own soldiers?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. All right. Now, then in the next paragraph, after a couple of sentences have passed by, you then refer to Mr. Sefer Halilovic. And I just want to ask you about a couple of aspects of this. What you said here is: "The chief of SVK, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, distanced himself from this incident and ordered me personally to gather as much information on the unfortunate incidents through operative work with other SVB members" and then there's a gap. Can you tell me what the word is in that gap, after the word "SVB members."

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see anything. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've just procured a photocopy, and I wonder if that could be given to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That might be easier to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's -- just to confirm, Your Honour, it's DD000255.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just take a moment and find the section I'm looking for. It's in the paragraph before the -- before the six proposals that you set out. It says: "Chief of Staff -- Chief of SVK, Mr. Sefer Halilovic, distanced himself from" --

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The members of MUP," it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So what that say -- the English translation here has got a word, "missing text." So we'll just rely on you here. What it says is that: "Sefer Halilovic distanced himself from this incident and ordered me personally to gather as much information on the unfortunate incidents through operative work with other SVB members and" and what do you say come there is? "Members of the MUP"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you then went on to -- the make certain proposals. And I'm going to come to those proposals in just a moment. Maybe if you keep that document there with you, because I'm just going to go back and clarify a couple of gaps with you that I asked you about earlier on. But I just want to ask you quickly about -- about what you said about Halilovic's -- Sefer Halilovic's order to you. Now, as you understood the situation, Halilovic was your commander by virtue of your membership in the -- in the inspection team of which he was the head and of which you were a mere member with SVB responsibility; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd object to that question. There is -- that's a multiple compound question. There's at least three questions there, maybe four. That's one that should be taken one step at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it -- it's amenable -- Your Honour, may I just say this. It's amenable of a single answer. But if it would assist the Prosecutor, I've got no difficulty in doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzankovic, I've got to ask you this question broken up into multiple parts, and that's what I'm going to do. So is it the fact that you were a member of an inspection team?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is it the fact that Sefer Halilovic was the chief of that inspection team?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is it the fact that because of that relationship, Sefer Halilovic was entitled to give you orders and you were bound to obey those orders? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: So, of course, when Sefer Halilovic gave you this order, which you've referred to in your report here, you were bound to obey it and you did obey it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that was within my power, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Of course. And as a member -- and I'll just -- this is just stepping outside this order for a moment, but this is a matter that may assist the Tribunal as well, and you can explain it. As a member of the SVB, you're aware that SVB members had a dual line of responsibility. They had to -- sorry, first of all, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you had to obey the lawful commands of your superior officer; in this case, Sefer Halilovic. But you also had an obligation to report up the professional line to another commander, that being Jusuf Jasarevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: After Sefer Halilovic issued you with the order, which is referred to in this document, to investigate the killings, after that time you did report up the professional line in a perfectly proper way to Jusuf Jasarevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And indeed all three of your reports, which you've given evidence about in this court, were directed not to Sefer Halilovic but up the professional line of reporting to Jusuf Jasarevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And, in fact, to your understanding -- well, I'll come to that question in a minute. I'll come to that later. I just don't want to lose the thread of this document now. So can we come back now to the document we're talking about. And I'm just asking you some questions about the instructions that you've detailed here that Halilovic gave you. You've -- you've mentioned here that you were ordered to gather as much information on the unfortunate incidents through operative work. And then -- and then it refers to "with other SVB members." Now, I wanted to ask you about that phrase "with other SVB members." At the time when Halilovic gave you this order, did he specify to you who the other SVB members were, or did he just put it in that general way, "work with other SVB members"?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say anything specific. He just said "generally with other members."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. And then he added to the term "other SVB members," "the MUP."

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, because Mr. Brankovic was there with me. And when I informed Mr. Sefer that we had been to the Jablanica SJB the night before that and that we had already done some things and that I had already sent out the first report and that Mr. Brankovic was helping me, then Mr. Sefer said, "Great. Then you can continue to work together."

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And, in fact, that is what you did.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come to what you did with Mr. Brankovic a bit later, but I now want to go through the -- the list of proposals that you made. Now, do you have in front of you that list of proposals, of which there appear to be six, although they're not numbered? Do you have that list in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to ask you about each one of these in turn, but could I put to you as a general proposition that of the proposals that you made, there were some that you were capable of -- of attempting yourself and there were some that just lay way outside of your powers to perform on your own; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of things were things that I could not do by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Well, I'm going to go through each one, and we'll see what could be done and what couldn't be. The first thing that you put on the list was: "To continue gathering operative information." Now, with respect to continuing gathering operative information, there were some things you could do and some you couldn't, I suggest to you. And I'll -- I'll be specific, and then you tell me if that's right. You were able to speak to -- well, perhaps I'll -- I'll ask you some specific questions about that gathering of operative information. First of all, you did take the steps of speaking to the local police and gathering what information you could from them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You're aware, for example, that Mr. Salihamidzic went and spoke to a number of civilian -- well, actually, I shouldn't use the word "civilian" because I'm not sure what their status is. But Mr. Salihamidzic went and spoke to the -- the two Pranjics, who had been rescued, and that was something you were aware of; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And -- and he also -- and this was part of your operative work, to gather that information from him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And you were also aware that he spoke to some of the guards, or at least -- a guard -- sorry, I take that back. You're aware that he spoke to a guard from the -- from the hydroelectric plant called Alija Turkic and interviewed him about what he knew or had been told; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That conversation with the people from the power plant is something that I was not informed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you recall an individual by the name of Halebic, Mr. Semsudin Halebic? Now, this is 11 years ago, I know, but I'm putting the person to you as a person who had an association with military security at the local level in Jablanica. Do you recall Mr. Halebic?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I've got a series of names I want to ask you about now. Is it -- and I'll just preface my questions about that with this: Do you recall now the names of all of the different people that you met in Jablanica back in -- in September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of all the people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Perhaps -- look, I'll put the individual names to you and see if you recall them. You don't recall Mr. Halebic. Do you recall a man named Nusret Sahic who was associated with the local military police in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met a gentleman in the 6th Corps, if that's him, and I met him in Konjic, but I never saw him or met him in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall an individual named Zajko Sihirlic, who was associated with the military -- sorry, with the security -- military security service in the 44th Jablanica Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is it -- these names that I've put to you, is it possible that you met them and you just don't recall it now?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps during my stay I met them once and I most probably forgot all about them, but if it was somebody whom I had actually worked together with, I would remember them. I remember people whom I worked with or saw frequently. If I just met a person on one occasion or was introduced to them, then I probably forgot about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzankovic, there's to be no prying into your personal life in any way here, and I just have to ask you one question: Did you have at that time a -- a family member who was missing who you were concerned about? I mean in -- in this period of -- of early September and perhaps through the period of September. I've just -- I've actually forgotten. I saw a note about it at one point. Was it -- was your mother missing?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she was not listed as a missing person. Her whereabouts were known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Look, I -- yes, I -- it's -- it's not necessary to go into any great detail about this. Was -- was the situation of your mother at that time causing you some concern?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father was killed, and for a long time I didn't know where she was, so it's natural that I was concerned about her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Can you just -- my final question about this -- or I've just got a couple of questions about it. When was your concern laid to rest about that?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even when I found out, I was still concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And just in general terms - I don't need to know the full details - but what was the problem about your mother? Was she unwell and you needed to find her, or what was the general problem?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother was in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And -- yes, my very last question about that: Was that the case during the time when you were -- was that the case throughout September of 1993?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the exact date when she was released.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I see. Is that a matter that was a matter of concern to you during the time when you were investigating these killings?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I was resigned at the time. I was resigned to it. My father was gone. I didn't know where she was. I had no family. I was constantly out in the field, while the others were permanently in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Well, I won't ask you any more questions about that topic, and thank you for answering those questions. Okay. Now, I want to persist with the list of -- of proposals that you made. So the first proposal that you made was "to continue gathering operative information."

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: The second proposal that you made was "to establish a mixed committee of MUP and SVB members headed by investigative organs to make sure to include doctors and other experts who will carry out exhumation of bodies and establish the causes of death," and then you indicated indications of savagery, cutting out of hearts, and slit throats. Now, I wanted to ask you about this. You saw that it was impossible to -- for you to assemble such an investigative committee in Jablanica and that you needed help and support at the very highest level from Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was impossible for me to assemble such a team. We didn't have such personnel in Jablanica, and also I didn't have the powers to issue any orders to effect something like that, and that is why I made a request to my superiors about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your hope and your intention was that Jusuf Jasarevic would bring this about; is that correct? That is, at the time when you sent this report off to Jusuf Jasarevic.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that the people in Sarajevo would take the necessary steps to assist in relation to this case. Who was supposed to do what and in what way, I'm not a military expert, so I can't give you my comment on that. But I was hoping that orders or people would come from Sarajevo to help to shed light on this and to bring the investigation to completion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, -- yes, and I'm not asking you to issue attacks on other people here either, Mr. Dzankovic. That's not the direction of the questions. I want to move on to the third topic, and that is the proposal to interview members of Adnan Solakovic's unit who were quartered in close proximity and must have seen at least part of, if not all of the murders and their perpetrators. "Do this upon the unit's return to Sarajevo in the context of the reasons mentioned in the report." Now, in fact, you yourself did make an effort to inquire of the -- of certain officers in the 2nd Independent Battalion when you went to Grabovica for a visit. And in particular, I'm thinking of your visit to Samir Pezo. But it's the fact, isn't it, that those individuals were simply unwilling to discuss what they'd seen when you asked them; is that correct? Let me ask that question again. It had a clause built into it that's unnecessary. Those individuals were unwilling to discuss anything about the crimes with you when you asked; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My attempt to discuss it came up against a wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And the people with whom you attempted to discuss it were indeed the two most senior people in that battalion; namely, Samir Pezo and Adnan Solakovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, you make no suggestion that these people were happy about what had occurred. In fact, to your opinion, they seemed to be very distressed and sad about what they'd observed, if they'd seen anything at all. Sorry, look, I withdraw that question. I keep building a clause into it. I apologise. These people presented to you as being unhappy and depressed about what had -- what had occurred in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you made the proposition that the Solakovic -- the members of Solakovic's unit should be spoken to back in Sarajevo because you thought that might be a more effective place to interview them, rather than on the terrain at Grabovica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The conditions would be better there, and also if they were called in by the chief of the military security service or if they received an order from a higher-up commander to come, then they would come. I myself, being in the position that I was in, was not able to tell or order anybody to come and speak to me. Up in Sarajevo this was something that could be regulated with an order, so that they would have to go and have to talk about the topic. The same thing was done in relation to the Trebevic I operation, where they had to go for the interview and provide the information requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. But your understanding was that when back in Sarajevo it would be other members of the SVB that would have that task to interview those people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole service was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And -- yes, I understand. The next proposal that you had was "To request a report from Zulfikar Alispago, commander of the Zulfikar unit." And you've indicated there that "Zulfikar Alispago, who as he himself says, wrote a report and forwarded it to the Sarajevo SVK." In communicating that particular proposal to Jusuf Jasarevic, what you were telling him was there should be a report sitting in Sarajevo from Zuka and you guys had better go and have a look at it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the essence. And if they didn't have it, then they would -- should look for it, to where -- wherever they -- he sent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And if they didn't find it, they could also request him to give them another copy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they could have contacted Zuka personally and asked him to send a copy to the military security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Just to be clear about that, at the time that the report -- at the time that you made this proposal, on the 13th of -- of September, to your knowledge Zuka had already departed for the front line with his soldiers to go into action; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, the fifth request was that "It would be appropriate to" -- sorry, I would just read it out to you without putting my words in. You proposed that there be a request -- "Request a written report from Commander Ramiz Delalic, also known as Celo, on the events in Grabovica village." Now, that was a proposal that was more realistic to be made -- perhaps I -- no, I take that back. I won't put words in your mouth. Did you mean by that proposal that such a request ought to be made of Ramiz Delalic when he returned to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that if a team was formed and comes from Sarajevo and it includes all the elements, including logistics support, then you could do all of those things down there. Since the team wasn't formed, all of this could be done in Sarajevo at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Could I just ask you this: Did you -- did it occur to you in your thinking at this time that although an inspection team was a very desirable thing, it might turn out that it just wasn't possible and that there would have to be further investigations back in Sarajevo at a later time? Was that a scenario that occurred to you at the time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection. He's asking him to speculate. In fact, several speculations. He's asking: Did it occur to your thinking at the time; it might turn out; it just wasn't possible. You're asking for multiple speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's absolutely wrong. I'm asking whether the witness adverted to the possibility that the team wouldn't come, and that's what the question, in my submission -- it may be a wit wordy, but it plainly says that and plainly means that. But if the Prosecutor wants the question to be put another way, I've got no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you might ask a very simple question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I try to -- I try to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But the question, then, is: Did it occur to you that it might be impossible for such a team to be sent from Sarajevo, given the realities of the war?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think about that, really. But it states here clearly: "Request a written report." You could also request the report by packet connection that same day, and you could ask Mr. Ramiz Delalic, Celo, immediately to send a -- a report. You can do that through communications. And nobody had to walk anywhere in order to carry this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you -- did you yourself know whether Ramiz Delalic was a person who replied to requests from the security organs?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he -- he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And finally, you made a proposal of applying strict censorship to the media -- I'll read the actual passage: "Apply strict censorship to the media exploitation of facts related to this incident because of the current military and political situation."

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, were you referring there to -- when you referred to "military" -- I'll ask you about military and then I'll ask you about political. In terms of the military situation, were you referring there to the fact that there was an upcoming offensive operation which, by the time of the 13th of September, had already commenced?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just that. I was thinking of the whole situation in the army where each moment was used in order to create discord amongst the three ethnic groups who were members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and there were people who would use any opportunity. If anything happened - and it's a fact that something happened here - to distort, blow it up, use it - and I thought the exploiting this information was something that you couldn't hide, because the information was already published in the media. In Jablanica, it was published. People knew about it. It was reported about. I asked for censorship simply because I didn't want anyone to use that information and to exploit the information. What I was thinking of was to actually have the information released after an investigation was conducted and proper steps had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And it appeared to you that this -- having regard to what you said just, it appeared to you that the crimes that took place in Grabovica would have been exploited by extremist elements among all the communities, Serb, Croat, and Bosniak; is that true?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Whereas, to your understanding, it was the policy of the army, and indeed of the Bosnian government, to fight to preserve a multi-ethnic Bosnia using a multi-ethnic army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was our aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And these killings were a total disaster for the Bosnian struggle, as far as you could see; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that, Your Honour. How can he - he is not a historian; he's not a political analyst - answer something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe this question is too broad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- I asked it because he was a participating soldier in the army at that time. But if the question is not assisting the Tribunal, I just won't persist with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. I think you may have answered my next question in advance. I was going to ask you about the political situation, but I take it that what you've just said referred equally to the military and the political situation. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean what you asked me about to preserve a multi-ethnic --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- democratic Bosnia and Herzegovina, then yes, that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, that was what I was asking you. Thank you. Now, that completes my questions on that document. I just have some questions now about the communications --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm -- Your Honour, I'm in the Court's hands. I'm just going to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's the right time for us to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Mr. Dzankovic, I'm moving into the -- the final session of this cross-examination now, and I just wanted to ask you some questions about the reporting and communications methods that you had available to you. When you issued your three reports that you did to Jusuf Jasarevic, physically speaking, how did those reports get transmitted to Jasarevic in Sarajevo? Were they sent on the paket veza system or some other way?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The package -- the packet system, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've heard of this from -- in various ways in this case, but would you mind just explaining to the Tribunal, what is the paket veza system and how does it work -- or what was the paket veza system and how did it work.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could understand, it's a type of protected communication which is sent through the computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Is it somewhat similar -- I understand this was back in 1993, but is it somewhat similar to the system of e-mails which exists now in modern telecommunications?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can tell, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if things -- I mean, in an ideal situation - I'm not suggesting in the concrete situation you were in - but in an ideal situation, when you sent such a message off from Jablanica to Sarajevo, how long should it take for the actual message to be sent? I'm not talking about how long it takes for somebody to read it or to notice it, but how long electronically did it take for the message to be sent?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly the time that it takes. As far as I know, generally, I would submit the message in written form, I would submit the piece of paper which I wrote by hand. This would then be typed into the computer, and it would be sent, as far as I knew, to the communications centre in Sarajevo. There were people there who received such messages or reports. Most probably they sorted them and forwarded them to the administrations or the people to whom they were addressed. That's what I know. As far as the speed and the time that it took for it to arrive at its destination, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I won't ask you for precise times. If -- if you sent a message in the morning, let's just say on a particular morning, not related to this case, but let's say on a particular weekday morning you had -- had you -- provided your written piece of paper to the computer operator and the operator then sent that message. Would you expect the telecommunications centre up in Sarajevo to receive that message the same day, or within an hour, or might it be a longer time? In other words, what's your best estimate of the transmission time for these messages?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it would take 24 hours to reach the person it was addressed to, taking into account the procedure, how it's sent, and the system, I assume that it would be received within 24 hours from the time it was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the previous answer, he says, "I couldn't tell you exactly the time that it takes," that's on page 39, line 8. Now he says "I assume," he used the word "assume" twice. It's nothing more than speculation and it should be stricken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may address this in your re-examination, because this is the answer from this witness. You may proceed, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, as to where -- as to the availability of communications equipment in Jablanica, is it the case that in -- in an office -- I withdraw that. I'll start the question again. In the main office of the TO Staff of Jablanica, was there such a paket veza computer available to be used by you?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And was that office -- you've indicated the location of where the IKM was. I bear in mind your comments about the IKM, but I'm just going to call it the "IKM" so we don't waste a lot of time. So in the office where -- in the building where the IKM was, was there also to be found the TO Staff office?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO Staff office, as far as I know, was not in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts was it? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The packet system was there in the building in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to explain. It was a complex of buildings. The buildings were all connected and the TO was in that complex, but the building where the IKM was was not in the same building as the TO Staff command, but the packet system of communications was in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me just be clear about that. Is it the fact that the -- the basement connected to a number of different buildings?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Prior to the establishment of the -- well, who else -- you -- perhaps I should ask you this: Who else used that particular paket veza system?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, except for the MUP - I can't say anything about them - but I think that this system was also used by other units, by the brigade command, by the TO. Most probably. I don't know. If something was urgent, then the civilian organs used it as well, because there was no direct communication with Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Right. I understand. And to the best of your knowledge, this particular paket veza computer that was located in the -- in the basement was the only one in communication with Sarajevo in Jablanica at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Are you able to remember the name of this complex of buildings?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in the directorate of the Jablanica hydroelectric power station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you've indicated that housed in that complex of buildings was the IKM and also the -- the TO. Do you recall who else or what other bodies were housed in that complex?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the others. I know that there was also a restaurant or a canteen in that complex where refugees and soldiers had their meals. I also took my meals there in that complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And you've also indicated that this complex was more or less across the street from the Hotel Jablanica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you recall who it was that provided guards or security for that complex of buildings, if anyone did?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I saw, other than the person at the reception who was at the entrance gate of the power plant, I didn't see any military security in that complex or around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And there was certainly no military police or other guards taking care of the IKM specifically, were there?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, there were none. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could you explain -- was there a telephone at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was there a conference room at the IKM?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only premises that we used and called the "IKM" was actually that conference room. That was the only room that we used. We didn't use any other rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, I bear in mind what you've said about the term "IKM" earlier, but fact is that the IKM was one room; correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Did you have a secretary or a receptionist there, or were you dependent upon the person who was looking at the paket veza system down in the basement?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the operator of the packet system there. The inspection team didn't have any staff to assist it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you remember who it was who employed the -- the operator of the paket veza system? Were they from the TO or were they from some other organisation, as far as you recall?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's okay. Do you recall whereabouts Suljevic, Bilajac, and Karic lived at the time when they were -- or slept at the time when they were sleeping in -- in Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they also had rooms at the hotel, but probably because of the work they were doing, for the most part they didn't actually sleep there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you yourself ever accompany -- or perhaps I should ask you this: There was an occasion you mentioned that you went up to Buturovic Polje. Did you stay up in that more-northern part on the night of your visit to Buturovic Polje, or did you come back to Jablanica on that night?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we came back very late at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you recall there was -- there was no paket veza computer at Zuka's base in Donja Jablanica, was there?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And did you personally see any other paket veza system while you were in Herzegovina? I don't mean in -- in the 4th Corps area in Mostar but in the Neretva Valley generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Now, there was a local telephone network in -- in Jablanica available to civilians and military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But that local network was incapable of ringing to Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Apart from those two forms of communication, did soldiers in the field sometimes use Motorola hand-held radios?

utterances.speaker: NAMIK DZANKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only means that was used out in the field where the combat activities were underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, what was the range of those hand-held radios?
